rationales: High forward and reverse rates make the equilibrium composition establish quickly.
High reaction rates do not make equilibrium take longer to establish.
A reversible reaction can still reach dynamic equilibrium when both rates are high.
High rates alone do not make a reversible reaction practically irreversible.
Lightning does not primarily drive a reaction between nitrogen and water vapour.
Oxygen and water vapour are not the main atmospheric components reacting to form nitrogen oxides during lightning.
Carbon dioxide and oxygen are not the principal pair involved in this lightning reaction.
Lightning provides enough energy for nitrogen and oxygen to react and form nitrogen oxides.
The mixtures will differ because the containers start with different amounts of the reacting substances.
In container B, some PCl₃ reacts with Cl₂ to form PCl₅, leaving less PCl₃ than in container A.
Container A does not have less PCl₃; it starts without Cl₂ to consume it in forming PCl₅.
The reactants will not necessarily be completely consumed because the reaction reaches a dynamic equilibrium.
A closed vessel allows CO₂ to accumulate, which opposes further CaCO₃ decomposition.
High temperature promotes decomposition, and an open vessel lets CO₂ escape, shifting the reaction toward CaO.
Cooling opposes the decomposition needed to produce CaO.
Cooling opposes decomposition, and opening the vessel does not compensate for the low temperature.
Equilibrium does not require complete conversion of reactants into products.
Equilibrium does not require a fixed 50% conversion of the reactants.
At equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant because the forward and reverse rates are equal.
Removing a product disturbs the equilibrium rather than being a condition required to attain it.
Opening the can lowers the pressure, so the gas’s solubility decreases rather than increases.
The gas is dissolved in the drink before the can is opened, so it is not simply insoluble in water.
The gas is dissolved under pressure and escapes when opening the can reduces that pressure.
High pressure increases the gas’s solubility in the drink rather than decreasing it.
The forward reaction produces a gas, so increased pressure does not favour it.
The backward reaction consumes gaseous CO₂, so increased pressure favours that side, which has fewer gas molecules.
The backward reaction is affected because it consumes the gaseous CO₂.
The pressure change shifts the equilibrium toward the side with fewer gas molecules.
When the forward and backward activation energies are comparable, both directions can proceed at appreciable rates, allowing reversibility.
A much higher forward activation energy would hinder the forward reaction rather than explain a readily reversible reaction.
A much lower forward activation energy would make the forward direction easier but does not by itself establish reversibility.
Zero enthalpy change is not a requirement for a reaction to be reversible.
Reversible reactions can be useful for large-scale preparation when conditions are chosen to favour the desired product.
Reversible reactions can be used industrially by adjusting conditions to obtain a useful yield of the desired compound.
A reaction need not have equilibrium far to the right to be useful, since products can sometimes be separated or conditions adjusted.
An equilibrium far to the left is not the only circumstance in which a reversible reaction can be useful.
At equilibrium, product concentrations remain constant as the forward and reverse reactions proceed at equal rates.
Products do not keep increasing when the system is undisturbed at equilibrium.
Products do not keep decreasing when the system is undisturbed at equilibrium.
The product concentrations remain constant rather than changing after some interval.
